tagline: Paul's urgent letter to churches tempted to add circumcision and the law of Moses to faith in Christ, and his defense of the freedom the gospel gives.
overview:
Galatians is the angriest and most personal of Paul's letters. Soon after he had planted churches in Galatia, a region of what is now central Turkey, other teachers arrived and told his Gentile (non-Jewish) converts that faith in Jesus was not enough: to belong fully to God's people, they must be circumcised and keep the law of Moses. Paul writes to call them back. He skips his usual thanksgiving, tells the story of his own call to show that his gospel came from Christ and not from Jerusalem, recounts a public clash with Peter at Antioch, and then argues from Scripture and from the Galatians' own experience of the Spirit that people are set right with God through faith in Christ, as Abraham was, and not by the works of the law.

The letter's last two chapters turn to what that freedom looks like. It is not license to do as one pleases. It is life led by the Spirit, which produces love, joy, peace, and the rest of the fruit Paul lists, and which bears other people's burdens. Paul ends by taking up the pen himself and boasting in nothing except the cross.

Few short books have mattered more. Galatians shaped the early church's decision that Gentiles need not become Jews to follow Jesus. It sat at the center of the Protestant Reformation, and it remains at the center of modern debates about what Paul meant by justification, faith, and the law. It is also a letter about a question every generation faces: what, if anything, must be added to Christ for someone to belong to God?
author: The letter names Paul as its author (1:1; 5:2), and almost no scholar doubts it. Galatians is one of the undisputed letters of Paul, along with Romans, 1 and 2 Corinthians, Philippians, 1 Thessalonians, and Philemon. Its autobiographical detail, its fierce personal tone, and its close links to Romans in theme and vocabulary all fit the apostle. Paul writes together with "all the brothers with me" (1:2), probably his coworkers where he was writing, though none is named. As was common, he likely dictated the letter to a scribe and wrote the closing lines himself (6:11).
date:
The date depends on who the Galatians were, and that question has two main answers. The North Galatian theory holds that Paul wrote to churches in the old ethnic territory of Galatia in north-central Anatolia, around cities such as Ancyra (modern Ankara), where Celtic tribes had settled in the third century BC. Acts mentions Paul passing through "the region of Phrygia and Galatia" on his second and third missionary trips (Acts 16:6; 18:23). On this view the letter was written in the mid-50s AD, perhaps from Ephesus or Macedonia, not long before Romans, which treats many of the same themes more calmly. This was the dominant view in the early church and among many nineteenth-century scholars, including J. B. Lightfoot.

The South Galatian theory, argued influentially by William Ramsay, holds that Paul wrote to the churches of Pisidian Antioch, Iconium, Lystra, and Derbe, which lay in the southern part of the Roman province of Galatia and which Paul founded on his first missionary trip (Acts 13-14). Many scholars today favor this view. It allows either a mid-50s date or a much earlier one. Some who hold it date the letter to the late 40s, before the Jerusalem council of Acts 15 (about AD 49), which would make Galatians Paul's earliest surviving letter. They point out that Paul never mentions the council's decision that Gentiles need not be circumcised, which would have settled the argument, and they identify the Jerusalem visit of Galatians 2:1-10 with the famine-relief visit of Acts 11:30. Others identify Galatians 2 with the council itself and date the letter after it. Each reconstruction has real strengths, and the letter's message does not depend on settling the question.
setting:
Galatia had been a Roman province since 25 BC, a large territory running from the Celtic tribal lands in the north down to cities in the south that had been planted or refounded as Roman colonies. The churches Paul addressed were made up mostly of Gentiles who had turned from pagan gods (4:8), perhaps with some Jewish believers among them.

After Paul left, other teachers came. Paul never names them. He speaks of people who are "troubling you" (1:7) and of "those who are agitating you" (5:12), and scholars often call them the agitators or the teachers. They were almost certainly Jewish believers in Jesus who held that Gentile converts must be circumcised (5:2-3; 6:12-13) and observe the law of Moses, including its calendar of holy days (4:10). Their case was not foolish. Circumcision was the sign of God's covenant with Abraham (Genesis 17), Jesus was Israel's Messiah, and it seemed natural that those who joined Israel's Messiah should take up Israel's covenant sign. They may also have claimed the backing of the Jerusalem church and suggested that Paul had watered down the message to make it easier for Gentiles. The same question was troubling the church at Antioch (2:11-14; Acts 15:1).
purpose: Paul writes to stop the Galatian churches from accepting circumcision and the law as a condition of full membership in God's people. To do that he defends his apostleship and his gospel as coming directly from Christ (chapters 1-2), argues from Scripture that the blessing promised to Abraham comes to Jews and Gentiles alike through faith in Christ and the gift of the Spirit (chapters 3-4), and shows that freedom from the law is not freedom to sin but freedom to serve one another in love by the Spirit (chapters 5-6). Behind the argument is a pastoral fear: that the Galatians, having begun by the Spirit, will try to finish by human effort (3:3), and that Christ will then be of no value to them (5:2).
story: Galatians belongs to the period of the church's life told in Acts 13-19, when the gospel moved from Jewish communities into the Gentile world and the church had to decide on what terms Gentiles belonged. The story behind it reaches back to Abraham, to whom God promised that all nations would be blessed in him (Genesis 12:3), and to the covenant of circumcision (Genesis 17) and the law given at Sinai 430 years later (3:17). Paul reads the whole history as a single plan: the promise came first, the law was a temporary guardian until Christ came, and now in Christ the promise to Abraham reaches the nations. Romans takes up many of the same themes at greater length a few years later.
christ: Galatians is about Christ from its first sentence, where he "gave Himself for our sins to rescue us from the present evil age" (1:4). Paul's whole life has been reordered by the moment God revealed his Son to him (1:16). His most personal confession is here: "I have been crucified with Christ, and I no longer live, but Christ lives in me" (2:20). Christ is the one offspring of Abraham in whom the promises are fulfilled (3:16), the one who redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us (3:13), and the Son whom God sent, born of a woman and born under the law, so that we might receive adoption as sons (4:4-5). The cross stands at the center of the letter and at its end, where Paul says he will boast in nothing else (6:14).
reading:
Galatians is a real letter written in a crisis: abrupt, sarcastic in places, full of feeling. Read it at one sitting to feel its urgency. Chapters 1-2 are narrative that works as argument, and chapters 3-4 are dense scriptural reasoning best read with the Old Testament passages open.

Its central terms are debated. The Reformation reading, classically set out by Martin Luther, who lectured on Galatians and prized it highly, understands justification as God's declaring a sinner righteous by grace through faith alone, and the works of the law as any attempt to earn God's favor by obedience. The new perspective on Paul, associated with E. P. Sanders's study of first-century Judaism, James D. G. Dunn (who gave the view its name), and N. T. Wright, argues that the Judaism of Paul's day was a religion of grace and covenant, not of earning salvation. On this reading the works of the law are especially the practices that marked Jews off from Gentiles (circumcision, food laws, Sabbath), and justification concerns who belongs to God's family as well as how a sinner is made right with God. Defenders of the Reformation reading answer that Paul's argument still rests on human inability and on grace as a free gift, and many interpreters combine elements of both. Scholars also debate whether the Greek phrase pistis Christou means faith in Christ or Christ's own faithfulness. Every side agrees that Galatians sets people right with God through Christ, not through circumcision or the law.

Two misreadings are worth avoiding. The letter is not an attack on Jews or on the Old Testament, which Paul quotes as God's word throughout; his opponents were fellow believers in Jesus. And its freedom is not permission for self-indulgence, which Paul rules out (5:13).

structure.title: Greeting and rebuke
structure.summary: Paul greets the churches without a thanksgiving and expresses astonishment that they are turning to a different gospel, which is no gospel at all.

structure.title: Paul's gospel came from Christ
structure.summary: Paul tells how he received his gospel by revelation, how the Jerusalem leaders recognized it, and how he opposed Peter at Antioch. The section ends with a statement of justification by faith in Christ.

structure.title: The argument from Scripture and experience
structure.summary: The Galatians received the Spirit by faith. Abraham was counted righteous by faith, the law came later and could not cancel the promise, and in Christ believers are God's children and Abraham's heirs. Paul appeals to their shared history and to the story of Hagar and Sarah.

structure.title: Freedom and life in the Spirit
structure.summary: Paul warns against circumcision, calls the Galatians to use their freedom to serve one another in love, contrasts the works of the flesh with the fruit of the Spirit, and describes how a Spirit-led community treats one another.

structure.title: Closing in Paul's own hand
structure.summary: Paul exposes the agitators' motives, boasts only in the cross, and declares that what counts is a new creation.

themes.title: One gospel
themes.body: Paul insists there is only one gospel, the message of Christ crucified and risen, and that it cannot be supplemented. Adding circumcision as a condition of belonging does not strengthen the gospel; it turns it into something else. His fierce language (1:8-9) shows how much he thought was at stake.

themes.title: Justification by faith
themes.body: A person is justified, set right with God and counted among his people, through faith in Christ and not by the works of the law (2:16). Paul grounds this in Abraham, who "believed God, and it was credited to him as righteousness" (3:6). How exactly to understand justification and the works of the law is debated between the Reformation reading and the new perspective, but the letter plainly makes Christ, not the law, the basis of standing before God.

themes.title: The law's place in God's story
themes.body: Paul does not call the law evil. It came 430 years after the promise to Abraham and could not cancel it (3:17). It was added because of transgressions and served as a guardian until Christ came (3:19, 24). Now that Christ has come, believers are no longer under that guardian. The letter's question is not whether the law is good but what time it is in God's plan.

themes.title: The Spirit and freedom
themes.body: The Galatians received the Spirit by hearing with faith, not by keeping the law (3:2). The Spirit makes them children who cry "Abba, Father" (4:6), and the Spirit, not the law, is the power for a holy life. Freedom in Christ is freedom from slavery, whether to pagan gods or to the law as a means of standing with God, and freedom for loving service.

themes.title: One people in Christ
themes.body: Because all who belong to Christ are Abraham's offspring, the divisions that once defined people no longer decide who belongs: "There is neither Jew nor Greek, slave nor free, male nor female, for you are all one in Christ Jesus" (3:28). The clash at Antioch (2:11-14) shows that for Paul the gospel is at stake when believers refuse to eat together.

keyChapters.why: Paul's astonishment at a different gospel and the story of his call, which establishes that his message came by revelation from Christ.
The Jerusalem meeting, the confrontation with Peter at Antioch, and the letter's central statement of justification by faith in Christ.
The argument from Abraham, the curse of the law borne by Christ, the law as a guardian, and the unity of all believers in Christ.
God sends his Son and his Spirit so that believers become sons and heirs; Paul's pastoral plea and the allegory of Hagar and Sarah.
Freedom in Christ, the warning against circumcision, and the works of the flesh set against the fruit of the Spirit.
